utility.name: None — no Google vendor utility; ChromeOS updates are built in and automatic (any extra utility is the OEM's)
sources: Google Support — Update your Chromebook's operating system (support.google.com/chromebook/answer/177889)
Google Support — Check your Chromebook's update schedule (support.google.com/chromebook/answer/9367166)
utility.what_it_does: Google provides no Chromebook equivalent of a vendor control centre. ChromeOS itself handles updates: per Chromebook Help, the device automatically checks for and downloads updates when connected to the internet, and the owner completes an update by restarting when the 'Update device' notification appears. Settings > About ChromeOS shows the current version and a manual Check for updates button, and About ChromeOS > Additional details shows the update schedule / final update date. Hardware-specific utilities, diagnostics or settings beyond ChromeOS, if any, come from the device manufacturer (Acer, Lenovo, HP, Samsung, etc.), not Google.

google.driver_bios_channel: ChromeOS automatic updates are the only channel — Google states Chromebooks automatically manage updates so the device has the latest software and security features; there are no separate user-installed Google driver or BIOS packages for Chromebooks. Manual check: Settings (select time > Settings) > About ChromeOS > Check for updates; a found update downloads automatically and applies on restart. Google notes Chromebooks receive 10 years of automatic updates (per its Auto Update policy page, with caveats for pre-2021 devices receiving extended updates).
setup_notes: Connect to Wi-Fi and restart when prompted — that is the entire update routine for a new owner; plug into power to avoid interruptions, per Google's tips.

Check About ChromeOS > Additional details early to see how long the specific model will keep receiving automatic updates — models differ, and a 'Final software update' notification means ChromeOS/browser updates (security, bug fixes, features) stop.
Work/school Chromebooks may show update notifications as recommended (blue) or required (orange) and can be admin-managed — Google documents this distinction in Chromebook Help.
Any OEM utility (e.g. a maker's diagnostics or settings app on a specific Chromebook model): not verified on official Google pages — check the OEM's own support site for that model.
google.warranty_registration: not verified on official pages — Google's Chromebook Help pages reviewed cover updates and update schedules, not warranty registration. Chromebook hardware warranty is the device manufacturer's (OEM's), not Google's; no Google-run Chromebook warranty-registration path was verified on support.google.com/chromebook in this research.

first_week_checklist.item: Check for BIOS / firmware updates early
first_week_checklist.detail: In the first week, check for a BIOS or firmware update for your exact model through the maker's own update utility or support site — never a third-party driver site. Keep the laptop plugged into AC power, save your work first, and do not turn it off, suspend it, or interrupt the update while it runs. Expect the machine to restart, possibly more than once, and leave it alone until it boots back into Windows normally.
first_week_checklist.more_info: Dell, Lenovo, HP, and ASUS (in its MyASUS app) all document this route — look the machine up by model name or service tag. The makers' warnings line up: Dell warns that turning off or disconnecting power during a BIOS update could harm the computer, Lenovo's instructions require an AC adapter and a charged battery and warn against turning off or suspending until the update completes, and HP says to run on AC power because a power loss mid-update could leave the computer unable to operate correctly.

first_week_checklist.item: Run operating system and driver updates
first_week_checklist.detail: Run your operating system's own updater in the first week and repeat until nothing more is offered: Windows Update on Windows, Software Update on a Mac, or Settings > About ChromeOS on a Chromebook. Then open the maker's own utility — Lenovo Vantage, Dell SupportAssist, HP Support Assistant, or MyASUS — for drivers and firmware the OS updater may not cover.
first_week_checklist.more_info: Windows: Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates, then Download & install anything offered and restart if prompted. macOS: Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update finds, downloads, and installs Apple software compatible with your model; Apple advises backing up your Mac first and letting installation finish without putting it to sleep or closing the lid. ChromeOS: a Chromebook automatically checks for and downloads updates when connected to the internet, and you finish by restarting when the notification appears; to check yourself, open Settings > About ChromeOS > Check for updates. Maker utilities close the gap the OS updater leaves — MyASUS System Update, for example, automatically checks and lists the items that still need updating.

rows.label: Your Chromebook is up to date

first_week_checklist.item: Review bundled trialware and remove what you do not want
first_week_checklist.detail: New Windows laptops commonly arrive with trial antivirus suites, trial office software, and promotional offers; remove what you don't want via Start > Settings > Apps > Installed apps > More (...) > Uninstall. Do keep the maker's own support and update utilities — later items on this checklist use them. If you remove a trial antivirus, you're not left unprotected: Microsoft Defender Antivirus turns on automatically when no other antivirus is installed and working.
first_week_checklist.more_info: What actually comes preinstalled varies by model and retailer, and no official source we checked publishes a per-model list — so check your own machine rather than trusting a generic 'bloatware' list. Microsoft also documents uninstalling from the Start menu and from Control Panel, and notes that some apps and programs built into Windows cannot be uninstalled. Defender also turns itself off again when another antivirus product is installed and working, so swapping protection either way is safe.

first_week_checklist.item: Battery first charge: skip the myths, use the maker's charge settings
first_week_checklist.detail: Fact, not myth: a modern lithium-ion laptop battery does not need an initial full discharge or a special conditioning charge before first use. Charge whenever you want, with no need to let it run down to empty first — Apple states this directly for its lithium-ion batteries. For a laptop that lives mostly plugged in, use the built-in charge-limit option your maker provides, if your model has one.
first_week_checklist.more_info: Apple explains that a charge cycle is cumulative — you complete one cycle when the total amount discharged equals 100% of capacity, not necessarily in a single discharge — and that capacity diminishes slightly with each complete cycle. The built-in options: on a Mac, Optimized Battery Charging reduces the time the battery spends fully charged, and a Charge Limit (macOS Tahoe 26.4 or later) can be set between 80% and 100%, though the Mac still occasionally charges to 100% to keep its charge estimates accurate. Dell's battery settings offer Primarily AC Use (the battery never charges to 100%), plus Adaptive and Custom start/stop levels, and Lenovo Vantage offers a Battery Charge Threshold / Conservation Mode on supported models. Lenovo's official pages don't state one uniform percentage across models, and HP doesn't settle a specific charge-limit percentage for consumer models, so check the setting on your own machine instead of assuming a number. No official page we checked uses the word 'conditioning' for a first charge.

first_week_checklist.item: Make a backup and create recovery media
first_week_checklist.detail: Do this while the laptop is new and working, not after something fails: on Windows, create a recovery drive on a USB stick and back up your personal files separately; on a Mac, set up Time Machine with an external drive and let the first backup finish; on a Chromebook, keep your files in Google Drive or on external storage. Recovery media reinstalls the operating system — it does not by itself protect your files, so the file backup matters just as much.
first_week_checklist.more_info: Windows: search for 'Create a recovery drive' and make sure 'Back up system files to the recovery drive' is selected; the process erases anything already on that USB drive, Microsoft recommends recreating the media annually, and personal files need Windows Backup or File History as well. Mac: the first Time Machine backup may take longer than expected, you can keep using the Mac while it runs, and later backups only copy changed files; macOS Recovery can reinstall macOS over the internet while keeping your files and settings. Chromebook: recovery removes and reinstalls ChromeOS and permanently erases everything on the device, so back up first if you can; newer Chromebooks can recover over an internet connection, and the Chromebook Recovery Utility on another computer can create USB recovery media. Some Windows brands also ship their own recovery environment on supported models — Dell's SupportAssist OS Recovery and HP's recovery / Cloud Recovery options — so one may already be on your machine.

first_week_checklist.item: Save your encryption recovery key somewhere off the laptop
first_week_checklist.detail: Before you ever need it, save your encryption recovery key somewhere off the laptop: Windows BitLocker keys can be saved to your Microsoft account, a USB drive, a file, or a printout, and a Mac FileVault key must be copied exactly and kept in a safe place. Don't store the USB or printout with the computer — together they'd let someone bypass the encryption. A Chromebook has no user-held key to save; access hangs on your Google Account, so keep its password and second-step verification working.
first_week_checklist.more_info: Find the Windows options under Manage BitLocker > Back up your recovery key; the file option can't be saved to the BitLocker-encrypted drive itself, and you can view a key saved to your Microsoft account from another device by signing in to Microsoft's recovery-key page. Microsoft states plainly that its support cannot retrieve, provide, or recreate a lost recovery key — if it's gone, it's gone. On a Mac, you choose when turning FileVault on: let your Apple Account unlock the disk and reset your password, or create a personal recovery key and not use iCloud; Apple says to record the key's letters and numbers exactly as shown and keep the copy somewhere other than your encrypted startup disk. For ChromeOS, Chromebook Help doesn't present a key-saving step — treat that as 'no key is offered to save' rather than a quoted Google policy.

rows.label: Printout — store away from the laptop
Personal recovery key — copy it exactly
Password — make sure you know it

laptop_parental_controls.core_principle: On all three platforms the controls attach to the child's account, not to the laptop. The child must sign in with their own child account (never the parent's account, never an administrator account) for any control to apply.

account_setup.detail: Google says it takes about 15 minutes: start at the Google Account creation page or inside the Family Link app, enter the child's name, the email address they want, and their birthday, then sign in with your own Google Account and give parental consent the way Google offers. This route is for a child under 13, or the applicable age in your country; the supervised account gives the child Search, Chrome and Gmail with parental controls.
account_setup.title: Create the child's Google Account

account_setup.detail: A child above the applicable age can create their own Google Account, and the parent adds supervision afterwards. Google states that above that age the child can also stop supervision; if they do, the parent is notified and the child's supervised devices are temporarily locked.
account_setup.title: Older children: add supervision instead

account_setup.detail: Use the child's supervised account to sign in. On a brand-new Chromebook the first account signed in becomes the device owner; a parent who needs to be owner signs in first, then adds the child as a user.
account_setup.title: Sign the child in on the Chromebook

account_setup.detail: On the child's Chromebook, open Settings; under Accounts, next to Parental controls, click Set up and follow the steps. Google notes the child and the device must be nearby and the child gives their consent during setup; the parent signs in to confirm. Parents then manage settings in the Family Link app on their own device.
account_setup.title: Add supervision on the Chromebook if needed

account_setup.detail: Install the Family Link app from Google Play or the App Store and sign in as the parent; some settings can also be managed at familylink.google.com.
account_setup.title: Get Family Link on the parent's phone

controls_available.detail: A daily limit for the device set as a weekly schedule (different school-day and weekend allowances), plus a Downtime schedule (called Bedtime in older versions) that locks the device, and School time schedules. Daily limits apply per device, not as one shared pool across the child's devices. Parents can grant bonus time for the day.
controls_available.name: Screen time

controls_available.detail: Per-app time limits for the Chromebook's apps, unlimited time for chosen apps such as school apps, and the ability to block an app entirely.
controls_available.name: App limits and blocking

controls_available.detail: Three levels under Family Link Controls > Content restrictions > Google Chrome: allow all sites; try to block mature sites; or only allow approved sites. Parents keep their own approved and blocked site lists, manage which site permissions the child can grant, and can approve or deny the child's requests for blocked sites.
controls_available.name: Chrome web filtering

controls_available.detail: Per Google: children signed in on Chrome OS cannot use Incognito mode and do not have access to apps and extensions from the Chrome Web Store; parents manage the websites the child can visit and limit the child's ability to grant permissions to websites; with try to block mature sites on, Chrome blocks most sexually explicit and violent sites.
controls_available.name: Built-in supervised Chrome differences

controls_available.detail: SafeSearch is on for supervised accounts and is managed by the parent in Family Link's Google Search controls; the child cannot simply switch it off.
controls_available.name: Search

controls_available.detail: Content restrictions by maturity rating per content type, and purchase approvals in four strengths: all content; all purchases that use the family payment method; only in-app purchases; or no approval required. Free content that needs approval is requested either by message (parent approves or denies from a notification) or in person (parent enters their password on the child's device). Google states purchase approval settings only apply to purchases made through Google Play's billing system.
controls_available.name: Google Play content and purchases

controls_available.detail: Supervised YouTube settings and kids/teens tools are managed through Family Link alongside the other Google services.
controls_available.name: YouTube

controls_available.detail: Family Link shows the child's app activity: how much time goes to which apps.
controls_available.name: Activity

controls_available.detail: Family Link can show a supervised device's location when the device is powered on, recently active and connected to the internet, and parents can lock or unlock the child's device remotely from the app.
controls_available.name: Location and remote lock

controls_available.detail: Parents can help change or reset the child's password, edit the child's account information, or delete the account, all from Family Link.
controls_available.name: Account safety net

enable_steps.detail: Child's Google Account created with consent, supervised in Family Link; child signed in on the Chromebook with the supervised account.
enable_steps.title: Complete account setup and sign the child in

enable_steps.detail: All controls below live under the child's profile in the parent's Family Link app.
enable_steps.title: Open Family Link and select the child

enable_steps.detail: Controls > Content restrictions > Google Chrome: choose the filtering level, then add always-approved school sites and any blocked sites.
enable_steps.title: Set the Chrome filter

enable_steps.detail: In Content restrictions: confirm SafeSearch under Google Search; under Google Play set maturity ratings and the purchase approval strength.
enable_steps.title: Set Search and Play rules

enable_steps.detail: Screen time > Time limits: turn on the daily limit, edit the weekly schedule, and add the Downtime (bedtime) schedule.
enable_steps.title: Set screen time

enable_steps.detail: Per-app limits for games, unlimited time for school apps, and block anything that should not be on the machine.
enable_steps.title: Set app rules

enable_steps.detail: Signed in as the device owner, open Settings > Privacy and security > Manage other people; turn off guest browsing and limit sign-in to chosen accounts, so the supervised account cannot be walked around with a guest session or another account. Setting names vary slightly by ChromeOS version.
enable_steps.title: Close the side doors on the Chromebook

enable_steps.detail: Sign in with the child's account: try a blocked site and send the access request, try downloading a free app and watch the approval arrive, and check the daily-limit display. Adjust, then hand over.
enable_steps.title: Test as the child

first_setup_checklist: Child's Google Account created with the correct birthday; parental consent completed
Account supervised in Family Link; parent has the Family Link app
Child signed in on the Chromebook with their own supervised account
Chrome filter level chosen; SafeSearch confirmed; Play ratings and purchase approvals set
Daily limit and Downtime schedule set; per-app limits for games
Guest browsing off and sign-in limited, from the owner's account
Tested while signed in as the child, then handed over
honest_limits: School Chromebooks are the school's, not the parent's: Google states Google Workspace for Education accounts can't be managed by Family Link and the school administrator decides which services a school account can access. If a school account is added as a secondary account under the child's supervised personal account, Family Link controls apply to it; if it is added as a separate user on the sign-in screen, Google states Family Link parental controls will not apply to that user account.

Family Link supervises accounts, and only on Google's platforms: Google's getting-started page states iPhones, iPads, and computers other than Chromebooks can't be supervised with Family Link. A Windows or Mac laptop in the same house needs its own platform's system.

The filter is a filter, not a promise: Google's own name for the middle level is try to block mature sites, and Google's Family Link app description says outright that Family Link does not make the internet safe. It shapes what the supervised account can reach in Chrome, not other apps' built-in content or an unsupervised account.

Side doors are account-shaped: guest mode and additional unsupervised accounts bypass supervision unless the owner restricts them; a Powerwash (factory reset) followed by setup under a different account removes the device from the supervised arrangement, so the owner account should stay in the parent's hands (reset point is framed guidance; guest/sign-in behaviour is documented ChromeOS functionality).
Purchase approvals have a hard edge stated by Google: they apply only when the child buys through Google Play's billing system, not to alternate billing systems or purchases elsewhere.

Supervision has an age exit: above the applicable age in your country, Google documents that the child can stop supervision; the parent is notified and supervised devices are temporarily locked, but from that point the arrangement is a family agreement, not a setting.

account_setup.detail: On the parent's device, open Settings (iPhone/iPad) or System Settings (Mac) > Family and create the family group if there is not one already. The organizer, and adults designated as parent/guardian, can create child accounts and set controls for children and teens in the group.
account_setup.title: Set up Family Sharing

account_setup.detail: In Family settings, choose Add Member, then Create Child Account. Enter the child's name and correct date of birth; Apple uses the date of birth to determine eligible services and to suggest parental controls such as Ask to Buy and Screen Time.
account_setup.title: Create the child's Apple Account

account_setup.detail: Agree to Apple's Family Privacy Disclosure for Children and the terms. Because child-privacy law (COPPA in the US, similar laws elsewhere) requires verifiable parental consent, Apple verifies the organizer's adult status; its legal disclosure names methods such as confirming the payment method on file (for example its security code) or an identity card in Wallet, varying by country.
account_setup.title: Verify you are an adult, and consent

account_setup.detail: Create the child's email address (Apple can create a free iCloud address if the child has none) and a password. The account joins the family group automatically. During setup Apple offers the first controls: age-related content restrictions for apps, books, TV shows and movies; Downtime and app limits; restrictions on who the child can communicate with; and approvals for purchases or free downloads.
account_setup.title: Finish the account

account_setup.detail: Apple's disclosure states that a child's account cannot be removed from the family unless the account is deleted, the child turns 13 (or the equivalent minimum age in your jurisdiction), or the child is transferred to another family; after that age the child may be able to keep the account without participating in Family Sharing.
account_setup.title: Know the membership rule

account_setup.detail: Give the child their own Mac user account as a standard user, not an administrator, signed in with their child Apple Account. The parent keeps the administrator account and password. If the child already has an Apple Account without consent, Apple documents adding it to the family via Invite in Person and agreeing to the Parental Privacy Disclosure.
account_setup.title: On the MacBook itself

account_setup.detail: Offered during account creation. Apple Support notes the age rules vary by region; in the United States an organizer can turn Ask to Buy on for any family member under 18, and for children under 13 it is on by default.
account_setup.title: Ask to Buy

controls_available.detail: Screen Time reports how much time the child spends in apps and on websites; with Family Sharing the parent views reports and adjusts settings from their own device.
controls_available.name: App & Website Activity

controls_available.detail: A scheduled time away from the screen (Every Day, or Custom days for school nights versus weekends), also switchable on immediately. The child is warned five minutes before downtime begins; calls and always-allowed apps stay available.
controls_available.name: Downtime

controls_available.detail: Daily time limits for individual apps, app categories and websites. When time runs out the child can request more; the parent approves or declines in Settings > Screen Time or in Messages.
controls_available.name: App Limits

controls_available.detail: The short list of apps that stay reachable during downtime and after limits, for essentials.
controls_available.name: Always Allowed

controls_available.detail: Web content level (unrestricted access, limit adult websites, or allowed websites only); Store Restrictions by age rating for apps, movies, music and books, plus preventing app installs/deletes and in-app purchases; and Game Center limits covering multiplayer games, adding friends, connecting with friends, private messaging, and avatar/nickname and profile-privacy changes.
controls_available.name: Content & Privacy restrictions

controls_available.detail: Limits on who the child can communicate with during allowed screen time and during downtime.
controls_available.name: Communication Limits

controls_available.detail: A Screen Time safety feature for child accounts that warns the child when photos containing nudity are sent or received in Messages and some other apps, blurs the image, and offers guidance and resources. Apple turns it on by default for child accounts in current versions.
controls_available.name: Communication Safety

controls_available.detail: A four-digit passcode the child does not know; it locks Screen Time settings and is required to grant more time. On current versions a parent can see when the passcode was last used and opt into a notification when it is used.
controls_available.name: Screen Time passcode

controls_available.detail: Purchases and free downloads the child initiates in the App Store, iTunes Store and Apple Books must be approved by the family organizer or a parent/guardian in the group.
controls_available.name: Ask to Buy

controls_available.detail: Optional: the child's device location can be shared with the family through Find My; enabling it is a choice offered when the child is added to the family.
controls_available.name: Location Sharing

enable_steps.detail: Child Apple Account created in Family Sharing; child signed in on the MacBook with their own account as a standard user.
enable_steps.title: Complete account setup and sign the child in

enable_steps.detail: On the parent's Mac signed in with the organizer's Apple Account (or on the child's Mac signed in to the child's account), open System Settings > Screen Time; with Family Sharing, choose the child from the Family Member pop-up menu.
enable_steps.title: Open Screen Time for the child

enable_steps.detail: So usage reports exist before limits are judged.
enable_steps.title: Turn on App & Website Activity

enable_steps.detail: A code the child does not know and that is not reused anywhere else.
enable_steps.title: Set a Screen Time passcode

enable_steps.detail: Turn on the schedule; use Custom days for different school-night and weekend hours.
enable_steps.title: Set Downtime

enable_steps.detail: Cap the biggest time-sinks; keep school and messaging essentials always allowed.
enable_steps.title: Set App Limits and Always Allowed

enable_steps.detail: Set the web content level and store age ratings; under App Store, Media, Web & Games, set Game Center rules if relevant.
enable_steps.title: Turn on Content & Privacy

enable_steps.detail: Set Communication Limits and confirm Communication Safety is on.
enable_steps.title: Review Communication settings

enable_steps.detail: In Family settings, select the child and turn on Ask to Buy if it is not already on.
enable_steps.title: Confirm Ask to Buy

enable_steps.detail: Sign in with the child's account, run into a limit, and start a download so the parent sees the approval request arrive on their own device.
enable_steps.title: Test as the child

first_setup_checklist: Family Sharing set up; parent is organizer or parent/guardian
Child Apple Account created with the child's correct date of birth; adult verification and consent completed
Child signed in on the MacBook with their own account, as a standard (non-admin) user
Screen Time on for the child, with a passcode the child doesn't know
Downtime schedule and App Limits set; Content & Privacy ratings set
Ask to Buy on; Communication Safety checked
Tested while signed in as the child, then handed over
honest_limits: The administrator password is the real lock on a Mac: Screen Time holds because the child is a standard user; a child who knows an administrator password, or holds an administrator account, can change accounts and settings (general guidance, framed as such; the account structure is Apple's documented pattern).

Without Family Sharing, Apple documents setting Screen Time by logging in to the child's own Mac account; that works on that Mac but nothing syncs to or reports to the parent's devices. Family Sharing is what makes controls remotely manageable and visible.

Content & Privacy web settings are Screen Time's own filtering for the Mac, not a whole-home network filter, and individual apps manage their own content on top of it; check the apps and browsers the child actually uses (framed guidance).

Ask to Buy covers purchases the child makes through Apple's stores with their account; it does not govern buying elsewhere, and Apple's legal disclosure notes some categories (for example re-downloads and redemption-code downloads) may not be subject to Ask to Buy.

Ages and defaults are regional: the age at which a child can leave the family arrangement, whether Ask to Buy is on by default, and which controls a region requires to stay on all vary by country, per Apple's support pages.

Erasing the Mac and setting it up under a different Apple Account takes it out from under these settings; the anchor is the child's account staying in the family and the parent keeping the only administrator credentials (framed guidance).

account_setup.detail: Sign in at account.microsoft.com/family with the parent's own Microsoft account. The adult who runs the group is the family organizer; organizers add and remove members, manage limits and permissions, view activity for members with reporting enabled, and give consent for a minor.
account_setup.title: Start from the parent's account

account_setup.detail: Select Add a family member and choose the role Member. Microsoft describes Member as usually the best option for a child; Organizer is the adult role. The same flow exists in the Microsoft Family Safety app (Add a family member > role > Invite to family group).
account_setup.title: Add a family member

account_setup.detail: Enter the child's email address or phone number to send an invite, or create a new Microsoft account for the child as part of the flow. The invitee signs in to their own account to accept. An account can belong to only one family group at a time.
account_setup.title: Invite, or create the child's account

account_setup.detail: If the child is under the statutory age for your country, they are prompted to request adult consent and the organizer approves it. Statutory ages vary by country (Microsoft publishes a country list), and some regions require additional consent steps; Microsoft's consent pages describe an extra requirement under China's PIPL as an example.
account_setup.title: Give consent if asked

account_setup.detail: On the child's laptop, go to Windows Settings > Accounts > Family, add or allow the child's account, and have the child sign in to Windows with their own account. Once they sign in, the device appears in their connected devices, which is what applies the family settings to that machine.
account_setup.title: Connect the laptop

account_setup.detail: Microsoft's own note: make sure the child's account is set as a standard user, because family features may not work properly if the child's account is an administrator. The parent keeps the administrator password.
account_setup.title: Keep the child a standard user

controls_available.detail: Daily time limit plus an allowed-hours schedule for the child's Windows device, settable per day of the week; one schedule can be shared across the child's devices (Windows, Xbox, Android). The child can request more time and the organizer grants or refuses. Microsoft notes screen time counts while the child is signed in.
controls_available.name: Screen time (device)

controls_available.detail: Per-app or per-game daily time limits and allowed windows across the child's connected Windows, Xbox and Android devices, plus the ability to block a specific app or game outright.
controls_available.name: App and game limits

controls_available.detail: In the Apps and games content filter, set the age up to which apps and games are allowed; content rated above that age is blocked or needs approval, and specific titles can go on a never-allowed list.
controls_available.name: App and game age ratings

controls_available.detail: Turn on Filter inappropriate websites and searches: mature websites blocked by default and Bing searches filtered, with parent-managed Blocked sites and Allowed sites lists, an Only use allowed websites allow-list mode, and an option to always allow educational websites. Applies only in Microsoft Edge while the child is signed in (see honest_limits).
controls_available.name: Web and search filtering

controls_available.detail: From the child's Spending page, organizers can require adult approval for purchases, add money to the child's own account balance instead of attaching a card, receive purchase notifications, and review spending activity.
controls_available.name: Purchases and spending

controls_available.detail: Organizers can view activity for members who have reporting enabled and a device added: device screen time, app and game activity, and the child's Edge searches and visited sites. Reporting is toggled per member, per platform.
controls_available.name: Activity reporting

controls_available.detail: Family Safety includes location sharing between family members, documented mainly around the Family Safety app on phones. Microsoft's pages consulted do not promise live location for a Windows laptop; treat location as a phone feature.
controls_available.name: Location

enable_steps.detail: Child added as a Member with consent given if prompted; child signed in on the laptop with their own account, set as a standard user.
enable_steps.title: Complete account setup and sign the child in

enable_steps.detail: At account.microsoft.com/family, select the child's tile, open the Windows platform tab, select Screen time, turn limits on, and set the daily limit and allowed hours for each day.
enable_steps.title: Set screen time

enable_steps.detail: On the same platform tab, open Apps, features, and games, turn on App and game limits, then set daily limits on, or block, the apps and games that matter.
enable_steps.title: Set app and game limits

enable_steps.detail: Select the child, choose the Edge platform, turn on Filter inappropriate websites and searches, and add specific Blocked sites or Allowed sites. For younger children, turn on Only use allowed websites and build the allowed list.
enable_steps.title: Turn on web filtering

enable_steps.detail: In Content filters > Apps and games, set the age rating the child may use without approval.
enable_steps.title: Set the age rating

enable_steps.detail: Open the child's Spending page; require approval for purchases, or add an account balance instead of a payment method.
enable_steps.title: Set spending rules

enable_steps.detail: Sign in with the child's account, open Edge, and try a blocked site and an over-limit app so the parent sees exactly what the child sees and how requests arrive.
enable_steps.title: Test as the child

first_setup_checklist: Parent (organizer) signed in at account.microsoft.com/family
Child added as a Member, with a Microsoft account of their own; consent given if prompted
Child signed in on the laptop with their own account, set as a standard user
Screen time limits turned on for the Windows device
Web and search filter turned on; child uses Edge while signed in
App/game age rating set; purchase approval required
Tested while signed in as the child, then handed over
honest_limits: Microsoft states it on its own filtering page: Family Safety web and search filters only work in the Microsoft Edge browser while the child is signed in to their Microsoft account. Filtering does not reach inside other browsers; Microsoft's documented answer is to block other browsers through App and game filters if that matters.
Microsoft states that app and game time limits do not work on websites; to limit a web version, use the Block related websites option in app limits or the web filter.
Everything follows the account: limits do not apply to a local account, to someone else's account, or while the child is signed in as an administrator.

A child with an administrator account, a second account, or the ability to reset the PC and start over is outside these controls (general guidance, framed as such; the account and standard-user points are Microsoft's own). Keep the administrator password with the parent.
Age and consent rules are country-specific: whether an account counts as a child account and what consent is required follow the statutory age where you live.
disclaimers: Dashboard labels drift: Microsoft has renamed these pages over the years (Content restrictions, Content filters, Web and search, Edge tab), so a reader's screen may use a sibling label for the same setting.
